questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: Reading a Score Against Its Group
questions.learningObjective: state what standardising a test's scores does to the numbers
questions.stem: A test is given to several thousand people, and each raw total is then translated using that group's own distribution. What has been done to the scores?

options.text: They have been standardised, so each one now reports a position in the group rather than a raw total
They have been weighted, so each one now counts for more in the total figure than before
options.misconception: confuses converting a score with giving its items extra importance

options.text: They have been cross-validated, so each has been checked on a second and separate sample
options.misconception: treats comparison against a reference group as a check of predictive power

options.text: They have been validated, so each now predicts the outcome the test was built to predict
options.misconception: treats translation against a reference group as proof of prediction

questions.explanation: A raw total is a number of points and means nothing on its own, since two tests can have different numbers of items and different difficulty and produce the same total for very different amounts of ability. Standardising fixes that by asking where each score sits inside the distribution the test actually produced, and it is that step which makes a figure like an intelligence quotient interpretable as a position rather than a performance. The weighting option fails because weighting decides how much each item contributes before the total exists, and nothing here is redistributed. The cross-validation option fails because cross-validation means testing a prediction on data held out from the fitting, which is a different procedure performed at a different point. The validation option fails because validity is a separate property, established by comparing scores against something outside the test, and a translation against a reference group establishes no such thing.
questions.hint: Ask what the raw number meant before the translation, and what the translated number means instead.

questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: What a Percentile Figure Reports
questions.learningObjective: state what a percentile rank reports and what it leaves unsaid
questions.stem: A child is told she sits at about the 84th percentile in her age group. What does that figure say, and what does it leave out?

options.text: That she scored above 84 percent of her group, and nothing about which abilities she has
That she has mastered 84 percent of the course, since the rank is a share of the syllabus
options.misconception: reads a rank within a group as a share of the material covered

options.text: That she is 84 percent as able as the strongest child in the group, as a direct ratio
options.misconception: treats a rank within a group as a ratio of two people's abilities

options.text: That her score has risen by 84 percent this year, since a rank records change over time
options.misconception: reads a position within a group as an amount of improvement

questions.explanation: A percentile is a statement about a comparison and a comparison needs a group, and everything about the figure follows from that. Saying 84th percentile tells a parent that the child is near the front of her class and nothing more, because the group is one class of one age in one place on one occasion, and a different group would give a different figure for the very same score. That is also why the figure says nothing about abilities, since a single total score is a summary and a pupil can sit high in the distribution on one measure and low on another. The mastery option fails because a rank among people is not a proportion of content, and the two come apart completely in a selective class. The ratio option fails because rank is ordinal, and an ordinal position cannot be converted into a ratio of ability, since the gap between the top and the next child may be much larger than the gap between two children in the middle. The improvement option fails because a rank is a snapshot and carries no information about where the child started.
questions.hint: Ask what a rank needs in order to mean anything, and whether it can say which strengths a person has.

questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: The Same Test on Two Occasions
questions.learningObjective: identify what a test-retest reliability coefficient describes
questions.stem: The same 100 people take a test on two occasions eight weeks apart, and their two sets of scores correlate at 0.86. What does that number describe?

options.text: Test-retest reliability, since it measures how far a score holds steady under repetition
Validity, since the test predicts a second administration so well the two are equivalent
options.misconception: treats steadiness across two sittings as prediction of a criterion

options.text: Internal consistency, since every item in the test agrees with the result of every other
options.misconception: describes agreement among items as though it were agreement over time

options.text: Norming, since the second set of scores has been mapped onto the first one's distribution
options.misconception: reads a correlation as though it were a conversion between distributions

questions.explanation: A test-retest coefficient answers one narrow question, which is whether the same person would obtain much the same score if the test were given again, and the eight-week gap is what makes the figure meaningful rather than trivial, since a gap of ten minutes would mostly measure memory for the answers. A high coefficient is a necessary condition for a test to be worth using and a sufficient condition for nothing, because a person could be perfectly consistent in the wrong direction. The validity option fails because the criterion in a validity study is something outside the test, such as a later measure of the thing, and a second copy of the same test is not that. The internal-consistency option fails because that asks whether the items agree with one another within a single sitting, and nothing here compares items. The norming option fails because a correlation describes how the two sets of scores travel together and not how one has been transformed into the other.
questions.hint: Ask what varies between the two occasions, and whether anything outside the test was compared.

questions.learningObjective: explain why a split-half coefficient understates a whole-test coefficient
questions.stem: A test's odd-numbered and even-numbered items give scores correlating at 0.71, which is below the 0.86 found by giving the whole test twice. Why?

questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: A Test That Is Consistent and Useless
questions.learningObjective: distinguish reliability from validity
questions.stem: A screening test gives nearly the same score to the same person every time it is given, yet those scores say nothing about how the person will do the job. What is wrong with it?

options.text: It is reliable without being valid, since consistency says nothing about predicting the criterion
It is valid without being reliable, since predicting the job should be enough to make scores steady
options.misconception: treats a failure to predict as though it implied a failure to be consistent

options.text: It is neither, because a test that predicts nothing cannot be given twice with the same result
options.misconception: assumes predictive failure rules out a consistent score by definition

options.text: Both properties are satisfied, since reliability and validity are two names for one property
options.misconception: collapses two distinct properties into a single one

questions.explanation: The two properties answer two different questions and a test has to pass both, so a test can pass the first and fail the second without any inconsistency in the situation. Reliability asks whether the instrument is steady, and validity asks whether it is measuring the thing it is being used to decide about, judged against something outside itself. A test that is reliably measuring the wrong thing is a familiar and serious failure, and it is more dangerous than an obviously erratic one because the wrong answers arrive in a tidy column. The valid-not-reliable option fails because predicting a criterion well is a different claim from being steady, and a test could manage the first by luck on a single occasion. The neither option fails because the description explicitly reports a stable score, which is the definition of reliability. The both-properties option fails because collapsing them removes the entire point of collecting both kinds of evidence about a test.

questions.learningObjective: identify content validity from a described item review
questions.stem: A driving test is passed by candidates who have never reversed a car, while the examiners report that the items sample driving well. Which kind of validity is in question?

Criterion, since the question is whether the score predicts a later measure of safe driving

options.misconception: treats a coverage question as a question about the underlying trait

options.text: Reliability, since the question is whether a candidate would score the same on a retake
options.misconception: answers a coverage question with a consistency question

questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: Whether an Instrument Measures What It Names
questions.learningObjective: state what a construct validity argument must supply
questions.stem: A researcher claims a new questionnaire measures anxiety, and shows that its scores rise alongside a physiological measure and predict who improves in therapy. What is at issue?

options.text: Construct validity, since the claim is that the instrument taps anxiety rather than something else
Content validity, since the claim is that the items sample the whole domain of anxiety
options.misconception: treats a convergent argument as a question about item coverage

options.text: Face validity, since the claim is that the questions look like sensible questions about anxiety
options.misconception: confuses how plausible the items look with what the instrument measures

options.text: Ecological validity, since the claim is that the scores predict behaviour in everyday life
options.misconception: reads prediction of a therapy response as prediction in daily settings

The face option fails because how reasonable the questions look is the weakest possible evidence, which is why it is named face validity and treated as a hypothesis to be tested. questions.learningObjective: state what a culture-reduced test can and cannot claim
questions.stem: A test removes all reading demands from its items and gives its instructions aloud. What has that bought, and what is still open?

It has removed cultural content from the scores, since no item now needs reading to answer
options.misconception: assumes removing one channel of culture removes culture from a score

options.text: It has shown the test to be unbiased, since nothing in it now needs the test's own language
options.misconception: treats the removal of one source of bias as proof that none remains

The unbiased option fails because no test has ever been shown free of content that some group finds unfamiliar, and the ambition is reduction rather than elimination. The identical-scores option fails because the same reasoning applies with more force, since language is only one way culture reaches a test.

questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: A Generation of Rising Scores
questions.learningObjective: state why a rise in raw scores over decades resists a single reading
questions.stem: Raw scores on a long-settled reasoning test have risen by about three points a decade in one country since the 1940s. What is hard about interpreting that?

options.text: Whether it reflects real change in the population, a change in the test, or who was sampled
Whether three points should be added to each earlier score to make it comparable with today
options.misconception: asks for a scoring adjustment where the issue is what the trend means

options.text: Whether the rise is larger in children than in adults, which would settle what caused it
options.misconception: supplies one comparison and treats it as though it settled the cause

options.text: Whether the same rise appears on tests of accumulated knowledge, since that is the whole puzzle
options.misconception: insists on a single named comparison that would resolve the question

questions.explanation: A trend line across decades is a description with several possible sources and nothing in the line itself picks one of them out, which is why the finding has been argued over rather than simply accepted. The candidate sources are genuinely different in kind. The test may be doing the same job now as it did in the 1940s or it may not, since norms, coaching, familiarity with test formats and the questions themselves have all changed. The population may have changed, through schooling, nutrition, smaller families, or through changes in who is actually tested. And the samples differ from decade to decade, so a rise in a sample is not a rise in a population. Each of these would produce a rising line and the line cannot separate them. The adjustment option fails because adding a constant to old scores would be a practical convenience rather than an explanation, and it would bake one of the candidate causes in as though it were established. The two other options each propose a single comparison and treat its outcome as decisive, and no one comparison is decisive while three explanations remain standing.
questions.hint: Ask what else besides the population could move a score on the same instrument over fifty years.

questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: What a Heritability Figure Is About
questions.learningObjective: state the scope of a heritability estimate and what falls outside it
questions.stem: A heritability estimate of 0.80 is reported for a trait in a large and fairly uniform population. What does that number not tell you?

options.text: How much of a difference between two whole groups would be attributable to genes, since the figure is about spread within one population
How much of the differences between individuals in that population runs through their genes
options.misconception: states the one thing a heritability estimate is about as though it were absent

options.text: Whether any of that genetic influence reaches the child through the environment the parents provide
options.misconception: treats a genetic route and a shared environment as one channel

options.text: How much room a particular individual would have to change the trait by changing their circumstances
options.misconception: reads a population-level statistic as a personal figure for one person

questions.explanation: The figure is a statement about how the variation within one measured population is divided between genetic and environmental sources, and both halves of that statement matter. The population is one group in one place at one time, the estimate describes spread within it, and the remaining twenty percent is not free of constraint, since the rest of the variation is shared by things in the environment that the study did not separate. What the figure cannot reach is a comparison between populations, and this is the single most common misuse of the number, because two groups can differ in a trait for entirely environmental reasons while the trait remains highly heritable within each group. The second option fails because it is the one thing the estimate is about, and dismissing it would leave the number with no content. The third option fails because genetic and environmental transmission are different mechanisms and a heritability figure does not merge them, since parents transmit both a genome and a household. The fourth option fails because a distributional statistic has no application to a single person, and an estimate of how much room there is to change something needs evidence about that person rather than a population.
questions.hint: Ask whether the comparison is within one group or between two, and whether the figure is about a person or a population.

questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: A Correlation That Shrinks Inside One Group
questions.learningObjective: explain range restriction as an artefact of sampling
questions.stem: A correlation between a test and later attainment is 0.55 across a whole school and 0.15 within a single year group of the same school. What does the fall indicate?

options.text: Range restriction, since a year group covers less of the scale than the whole school does
Regression to the mean, since a year group's scores should drift towards the school mean
options.misconception: describes a narrowing of the sample as though scores were drifting

options.text: Reliability, since the within-group figure must come from a less reliable measure
options.misconception: treats a smaller correlation as though it reported steadiness

options.text: A confound, since the year group must differ in ability as well as in spread of scores
options.misconception: invents an ability difference where the sample is only narrower

questions.explanation: A correlation is computed from the spread of scores on both measures, and a correlation computed inside a narrow slice of a distribution is not the same quantity as one computed across the whole, so the two figures are not directly comparable. The reliability option fails because reliability is estimated from repeated administrations of the same measure and says nothing about the spread of the sample it is applied to. The confound option fails because the year group comes from the same school, so there is no separate selection of more able pupils, and the difference between the figures is accounted for by the spread.
questions.hint: Ask how much of the score range each sample covers, and whether a correlation depends on it.

questions.learningObjective: state what a waitlist control does and does not control for
questions.stem: In a trial, 60 of 80 patients given a therapy improve and 30 of 80 on a waiting list improve. Which reading is right?

options.misconception: calls a weak control the strongest one without saying what it fails to control

options.misconception: dismisses the finding on a ground the record does not raise

options.text: The therapy is ineffective, since two groups this large would improve as many on their own
options.misconception: converts a control group's improvement into proof of no treatment effect

The chance option fails because the record raises no question about allocation, and a study need not be perfect to be worth reporting. questions.hint: Ask what the two groups shared and what they did not, and what each shared part controls for.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: One Injection Judged Two Ways
questions.learningObjective: explain what a two-factor pattern supports and what it leaves open
questions.stem: The same injection is called mildly uncomfortable by one person and terrifying by another, and the difference tracks how activated each was beforehand. Explain what that pattern supports and what it cannot settle.

answer.exemplar: The pattern supports the account that needs two ingredients rather than one, and the way to show that is to notice which two things are being manipulated. The situation is held constant, so it cannot be doing the differentiating, and the bodily state differs between the people, so it is the variable that tracks the difference in the experience. An account in which an undifferentiated bodily state acquires a label by being read against the situation predicts exactly this, since the person who arrives more activated reads the same needle through a more activated state and calls it worse. It also explains the puzzling cases in which a person feels uneasy with no cause to name, since the bodily condition is present and the situation supplies only a weak or absent explanation. What the pattern cannot settle is the mechanism on the bodily side, and this is worth saying plainly because the temptation to over-read a two-factor result is strong. The pattern is equally compatible with a bodily state that is itself more sensitive in some people, with a difference in how much the two of them attend to internal states, and with differences in what the injection meant to them in the past. It also cannot show that labelling is a single step, since a person might read a bodily state and then reinterpret it, and the description has no way of seeing whether that happened. A design that would sharpen the account is one that varies the body's activation and the situation separately across four conditions, including a calm state in a frightening setting, because a label account predicts that the same body state read against two different situations produces two different feelings, while an account resting on bodily state alone does not. What would count against the account is a finding that the label of the situation changes nothing once bodily activation is matched, since that would remove the reading step and leave the bodily state to do the work on its own.

questions.explanation: The answer has to identify the two ingredients, use the constant situation and the varying bodily state as the evidence, list rival mechanisms the pattern is equally compatible with, and propose a design that varies the two ingredients independently.
questions.hint: Ask which two things the situation supplies and which the body supplies, and which of them was varied here.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: What a Score Can Decide For a School
questions.learningObjective: state the boundary between what a test score supports and what it cannot settle about a pupil
questions.stem: A school is deciding whether to put pupils into separate classes on the basis of a score. Explain what such a score can support, and what it cannot settle about any individual pupil.

answer.exemplar: The strongest thing the score can support is a statement about a group, and the strongest thing it cannot support is a statement about the destiny of a child, and the gap between those two facts is the whole problem. At the group level a score is informative because pupils in a year differ measurably in performance and grouping by performance tends to produce classes that are more similar in attainment, which may be administratively convenient. What the score cannot do is establish what any one pupil is capable of, and the reasons are worth setting out one at a time. A score is a summary of one performance on one day on items that sample a domain incompletely, so some of what a pupil can do is not in the number at all. A score is a position within a comparison group, so it says nothing about how that pupil would perform in a different group, and a year group with a narrow range of ability will produce a compressed set of scores that misleads in both directions. And a score is a measurement with error, so two pupils with the same score can differ considerably in the ability the score is trying to capture, which means the cut-off at the boundary of a class is being applied to noise as much as to signal. There is also a feedback route that makes the first error compound, since a pupil placed in a class on the strength of one score is then taught the class is for, and the score is re-measured in a setting that has already been shaped by the first measurement. What a school can defensibly do is use several measures over time, keep the grouping loose and revisitable, and treat the score as one piece of evidence among many. What it cannot defensibly do is tell a pupil that a number has established what they will achieve, because no measurement of this kind can carry that claim.

questions.explanation: The answer has to separate the group-level use from the individual-level inference, and give at least three reasons the individual inference fails, including the error in any single measurement and the way a class's identity feeds back into later scores.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of claim a score licenses about a group, and then what it would take to license a claim about a child.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: Two Reviews Reaching Opposite Conclusions
questions.learningObjective: explain how methodological choices can produce a large disagreement about therapy effectiveness
questions.stem: One review concludes that talking therapies beat no treatment, and another that the benefit is far smaller than the first implies. Explain the choices that could produce that gap.

answer.exemplar: A gap between two summaries of the same literature is rarely a mystery, and the productive way to approach it is to list the decisions that were made differently and ask which of them could move the number by as much as the gap. The comparison group is the largest lever of all, because a therapy measured against a waiting list is being compared with doing nothing, which flatters it, and the same therapy measured against a group that received the same attention without the specific technique is being compared with something more demanding and looks smaller. A waiting list also lets the comparison group improve on its own, which pushes the measured gap down for a different reason, and the two effects can partly cancel, which is precisely why the choice is consequential. The outcome measure is the second lever, since a self-report scale that a patient completes at the end of therapy invites expectancy effects and a clinician's rating invites a different set of them, and a measure of symptoms may move without a measure of functioning moving. Whether patients and assessors were kept unaware of which arm they were in is a third, and in a therapy trial the expectation of help is itself a plausible cause of improvement, so an unblinded comparison cannot separate the technique from the expectation. The timing of the outcome measure matters too, since a benefit measured at the end of treatment and a benefit measured a year later are different quantities and studies often report the shorter. And the number of studies and their quality are not a single thing, since a literature with many small studies of variable quality tends to produce larger average effects than a smaller set of careful ones. None of this settles whether talking therapies help, which they do, and the honest conclusion is that the size of the benefit depends on what it is being compared with and how it is being measured. What would be worth having is a report that states the comparison condition, the blinding, the timing and the quality of the included studies alongside the figure, because a number quoted without those is not interpretable.

questions.explanation: The answer has to name at least four methodological levers, including the comparison condition, the outcome measure, blinding and the timing of measurement, and explain how each could move an average effect size.
questions.hint: Ask what the therapy was compared against, how the outcome was measured, and who knew which arm a patient was in.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: The Feeling That Does Not Go Away at Work
questions.learningObjective: weigh two accounts of emotional labour against a reported pattern
questions.stem: A nurse who feels irritated with a colleague speaks calmly and shows nothing at work, and is irritable with her family that evening. Explain what the accounts of emotional labour add, and what the case cannot settle.

answer.exemplar: The case is a familiar one and the two accounts that are usually offered for it point in different directions, and being clear about both is the whole task. The first account treats what the nurse did as an outward performance with nothing behind it, so the irritation is still there when she gets home and has nowhere else to put it, and the evening irritability is the displaced residue of a feeling the working day gave her no permitted way to express. The second treats the calm at work as evidence that the feeling genuinely diminished, on the grounds that sustained display of an expression is itself work and that suppressing an expression consumes resources which can themselves leave a person depleted by the end of a shift. The case as described leans towards the first, because the irritation is stated to be present at work and reported again at home, but it does not establish the first, and the reason is that the two accounts make different predictions about the timing and the pattern of the evening. The displacement account predicts an evening irritability that is out of proportion and that arrives at home, while the diminishment account predicts a general lowering of the person's capacity that is not specifically about the colleague. A nurse who was irritable at home on a day she had not worked with that colleague, or who reported a general flatness rather than an irritation, would be evidence of the second. Other things also remain open. The account cannot say what the colleague did or whether the irritation was reasonable, since the accounts are about what happens to a feeling after it has been withheld rather than about whether it should have been. It cannot say how long the pattern lasts, since a single evening is far too short to distinguish a settling effect from an accumulating one. And it cannot rule out ordinary tiredness, poor sleep or a difficult journey home, any of which would produce an irritable evening without anything about emotion being displayed. A design that would help would measure the nurse's own reported state at several points across a shift, along with physiological measures, and compare shifts on which she did and did not have to manage her expression, since the accounts disagree about what should be found inside the shift as well as after it.

questions.explanation: The answer has to state both accounts as they make it, use the reported evening pattern to lean towards one of them, give a distinguishing prediction, and list at least two things the case cannot settle.
questions.hint: Ask what each account predicts about the nurse's state during the shift, and whether the case reports any of it.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: Testing an App for Reducing Anxiety
questions.learningObjective: design a controlled trial for a digital intervention
questions.stem: A hospital wants to know whether a four-week mood-tracking app reduces reported anxiety in adults referred for anxiety problems. Design a study that can settle it.

answer.exemplar: Randomly allocate referred adults to the app or to a control group that keeps the same contact and the same schedule of assessments, give both groups the same information about taking part, measure anxiety with the same instrument at the same four points, and keep the person rating the questionnaires unaware of which group each participant is in. Then report the change over time in both groups against each other, along with how many dropped out of each, and say in advance which differences would count as the app helping and which would not.

questions.explanation: The design has to settle the question rather than merely produce a change, which means it needs a comparison group that controls for attention, for the passage of time and for the natural course of the problem, along with random allocation so the two groups are not built differently before the app is introduced. Masking the person who scores the questionnaires removes one source of expectancy from the measurement, and reporting attrition matters because a design in which the app's users are the ones who stay in the study has produced a result about who tolerates the app as much as about whether it works. An active control carrying equal contact is worth preferring over a waiting list here, since it is the attention and the expectation of help that would otherwise be credited to the app.
questions.hint: Ask what the comparison group has to match, who should not know which group a participant is in, and what happens to people who leave.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: Showing What a Reasoning Score Really Depends On
questions.learningObjective: design a study to test whether a score loads on an unintended ability
questions.stem: A test maker suspects a new reasoning test scores partly on processing speed rather than on reasoning. Design a study that can show what the score actually depends on.

answer.exemplar: Give the same items in three conditions that vary only the time allowed, so that the items are identical and the time pressure is not, and add a separate untimed measure of processing speed for each participant. Then report how much of the variance in the test score is accounted for by the timed and untimed conditions separately, and by the independent speed measure once reasoning is held constant, so that the loading of speed on the score can be seen directly.

questions.explanation: The question is which abilities the score varies with, and a correlational design alone answers it only if the candidate abilities are measured independently and the test is not confounded with them. Varying the time allowance while holding the items constant is what makes speed separable from reasoning here, because the same reasoning is required in all three conditions and only the pressure changes. Including an independent speed measure matters for a second reason, since it lets the analysis ask whether the test's dependence on time is the same as a general dependence on being fast, or whether the time allowance is doing something specific to this kind of item. Reporting the variance accounted for separately is the part that makes the result interpretable, and it is also what a reader needs in order to judge how much of the score is the ability the test claims to measure.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be held identical for speed to be separable from reasoning, and what else has to be measured independently.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: Claims About Reliability and Validity
questions.learningObjective: evaluate claims about the properties of a measuring instrument
questions.stem: Four claims about measuring instruments are offered. Which two of them are supported? Select both.

options.text: A perfectly reliable instrument can still be invalid for the decision it is being used to make
Whether the items sample the whole of a domain is a question settled by comparing scores with an outcome
A high reliability figure means an instrument is measuring the ability it is named after
options.misconception: confuses consistency of a score with the correctness of what it measures

options.text: A correlation computed within one year group estimates the same quantity as one across a whole school
options.misconception: assumes a correlation is unaffected by how much of the scale the sample covers

questions.explanation: The first supported claim is the one that matters most in practice, since a person can be measured very consistently in the wrong direction, and an instrument like that produces tidy data about something the decision does not care about. Consistency and correctness are different questions and both have to be answered before an instrument is trusted. The second supported claim is worth reading closely, because it is a claim about which kind of validity is being invoked rather than about a particular instrument, and its content validity is established by expert judgement against a statement of the domain while its criterion validity is established by comparison with an outcome, so the two are not interchangeable procedures. The third option fails because it collapses the two properties into one, and a high reliability figure is silent about what the score varies with. The fourth option fails because a correlation depends on the spread of scores in the sample, and a single year group covers a narrower slice of the scale and so yields a smaller figure for what may be the same underlying relationship.
questions.hint: Ask which question each claim is answering, and whether the answer to one settles the other.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: Claims About Shortcuts in Judgement
questions.learningObjective: evaluate claims about the heuristics people use under time pressure
questions.stem: Four claims about judgement under time pressure are offered. Which two of them are supported? Select both.

options.text: A shortcut is useful in ordinary life and still produces systematic errors in the laboratory
Deliberating for longer always removes the errors that a shortcut produced
A shortcut only operates when a person has no time at all, and disappears when a little time is given
options.misconception: claims a sharp switch between a shortcut and a careful judgement at zero time

options.text: People who know a shortcut exists are immune to it once they have been told about it
options.misconception: assumes naming a bias removes the bias it names

questions.explanation: The first supported claim is the one that keeps the topic from being a list of failings. A shortcut is a rule of thumb that has served people well, and using one to judge how often something happens, or how similar a case is to a known case, is efficient in the ordinary world where the base rates are stable and there is no time to count anything. The systematic errors show up when the shortcut is asked to do a job it is not suited to, such as estimating rare events from vivid examples. The second supported claim is a claim about the effect of time and it needs stating precisely, because the evidence is that giving people more time and letting them think reduces many errors without removing them, and some shortcuts survive any amount of deliberation because the information they need is simply not available to anyone. The third option fails because there is no switch at zero time, and a person with plenty of time will still use a shortcut on a problem they find easy to picture. The fourth option fails because telling people about a bias does not reliably protect them from it, which is one of the more discouraging and better-replicated findings in this area.
questions.hint: Ask whether a shortcut is a failure or a useful rule, and whether more thinking time is the same as the right information.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: Claims About Emotion
questions.learningObjective: evaluate claims about the main accounts of emotion
questions.stem: Four claims about emotion are offered. Which two of them are supported? Select both.

options.text: The accounts disagree about whether the body's response comes before the feeling or arrives with it
A bodily state that feels the same in two situations can be given different names by those situations
The accounts differ only in their vocabulary, and all of them predict the same sequence of events
options.misconception: denies that accounts which predict different sequences are rivals at all

options.text: Controlling an expression reliably removes the feeling that the expression was showing
options.misconception: assumes managing a display is the same as eliminating a feeling

questions.explanation: The first supported claim is a description of the disagreement itself and it is worth being able to state it, because the accounts are usually taught as a sequence and the sequence is exactly where they part. One account makes the body's response the source of the feeling, which requires the body to come first, and the account that refuses any ordering has both arriving from a common process, and these are incompatible claims that can be tested against the order in which people report feeling and bodily change. The second supported claim is the observation that motivates the reading step, since the same bodily condition is reported as different feelings depending on what is going on, and a raised heart is a preparation for several things at once. The third option fails because it denies that the accounts are rivals, and two positions that predict the same events are not in competition. The fourth option fails because managing an expression and eliminating a feeling are different operations, and a person can hold a feeling with no outward sign at all, which is a common and unremarkable experience.
questions.hint: Ask what each account predicts about the order of the body's change and the feeling, and what two situations do to one bodily state.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: Claims About Evaluating a Treatment
questions.learningObjective: evaluate claims about what a treatment trial can establish
questions.stem: Four claims about what a treatment trial can establish are offered. Which two of them are supported? Select both.

options.text: The comparison condition decides what part of any improvement can be credited to the treatment
How many participants leave a trial tells you something about who tolerated the treatment
A patient who feels better after treatment has thereby shown the treatment caused the change
options.misconception: treats improvement after a treatment as proof the treatment produced it

options.text: A treatment that helps in a trial has been shown to help the next patient who is given it
options.misconception: assumes an average result from a trial settles an individual case

questions.explanation: The first supported claim is the pivot of the whole enterprise, because a treatment is only ever measured by contrast with something else and the contrast supplies whatever the treatment is being credited with. A comparison that shares the attention but not the technique credits the technique, a comparison with a waiting list credits the technique plus the attention and the expectation, and a comparison with another technique separates them. The second supported claim is the one most often left out of a summary and it is a real feature of the evidence rather than a footnote, since people who drop out of a trial are rarely a random sample of those who entered, and if the treatment is the reason they left then the trial has described the treatment's tolerability as much as its benefit. The third option fails because feeling better after a treatment is exactly what would be expected from spontaneous recovery, from the natural course of the problem, and from the expectation of help, and a comparison is what rules those out. The fourth option fails because a trial reports an average across people, and any individual case is one draw from a distribution whose width the trial can also describe but not resolve in advance.
questions.hint: Ask what the treatment was compared against, and who is not in the sample by the end.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: The Order in Which a Test Is Built
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of developing and validating a measuring instrument
questions.stem: Put these five events in the order in which a new test is built, tried and put into use.

options.text: The domain the test is meant to cover is written down as a clear statement of what counts
Items are written to sample that domain and are then reviewed by people who know the subject
The items are tried on a small group and the awkward ones are revised or dropped
The test is given to a large reference sample so that raw scores can be converted to positions
The finished test is checked on a fresh sample against whatever outcome it is meant to predict

questions.explanation: The sequence runs from the domain outwards, and the order is a matter of dependencies rather than of convention. The statement of the domain has to come first because it is what the items are judged against, and a coverage argument cannot be made until there is a coverage to argue about. Item writing and expert review follow together, since the review is meaningless before the items exist, and it is the review that catches questions asking for something other than what was intended. The small trial comes next and is where the practical problems surface, since an item nobody understands or that turns out to need reading it is not supposed to is found here and not in the reference sample. Norming on a large sample then makes the scores interpretable, and it has to follow the revision stage, because norms collected on items that are about to change describe a test that will not exist. The final check on a fresh sample is last for a specific reason: a predictive figure obtained on the same people who shaped the test is inflated, which is the generalisability problem in its purest form. The order that puts the reference sample before the small trial fails because a small trial exists to change things, and anything normed before that describes a superseded test. The order that puts the predictive check before norming fails because a comparison against an outcome needs interpretable scores to make sense of, and because the fresh sample is meant to be untouched by the building process.
questions.hint: Start with what the test is meant to cover, then build, try, norm and only then check against an outcome.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: The Order in Which a Labelled Feeling Arises
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps of a two-factor account of emotion
questions.stem: Put these five events in the order in which the account that needs a label says a fear comes about.

options.text: Something happens in the surroundings that the person notices, such as a car swerving
The body responds, and the person detects a change of state without yet naming it
The situation is read together with that bodily change and the change is given a name
The named feeling takes hold as fear, distinct from the undifferentiated arousal
The feeling leads to action and expression that are characteristic of being afraid

questions.explanation: This account is distinctive precisely because it refuses to let a feeling emerge from the body alone, and the sequence is the argument. The event comes first because there has to be a situation for the reading step to read against, and the body's response comes second because the account requires an undifferentiated state to begin with rather than a feeling. The third step is where the account earns its name, since the bodily change is interpreted against the situation and that interpretation is what turns a raised heart into fear rather than into anger or relief, and the fourth step records the result of that naming as a feeling distinct from the raw arousal. The fifth step is the ordinary consequence, and it is last because the behaviour is a consequence of the feeling and not the source of it. The order that places the naming before the bodily change fails because the account's whole point is that a bodily state without a name is not yet a feeling, so there would be nothing for the naming to attach to. The order that places the action before the feeling fails because the account makes the behaviour a consequence, and an account in which the behaviour produced the feeling is a different account with different consequences.
questions.hint: The account needs an event, an unnamed bodily state, a reading of one against the other, and only then a feeling.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: The Order of a Graded Course Against a Fear
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps of a behavioural programme for a fear
questions.stem: Put these five events in the order in which a graded programme for a fear runs from start to finish.

options.text: The feared situations are listed and ranked by how manageable they look to the person
The person learns a way of relaxing that can be used inside the feared situation itself
The easiest situation on the list is approached and stayed in until the anxiety falls
The next situation up is approached in the same way, and the steps continue upward
The hardest situation is managed without relapse and the plan is set to be repeated

questions.explanation: The programme is a ladder and the order is what makes it climbable, so each step depends on the one before. The list comes first because the difficulty has to be known before anything can be ordered, and having the person do the ranking matters since a step that looks manageable to the client is a step that will be attempted. Learning a way of relaxing comes next, and it comes before the first approach rather than after, because the technique has to be available inside the situation where it is needed and not only in the clinic. The third step is the first approach and staying until the anxiety has fallen is the whole mechanism, since the expectation being tested is that the fear will rise and then come down on its own, and leaving at the peak of the anxiety would teach nothing. The remaining steps move upward only after the previous one holds, which is what stops the programme becoming a series of failures. The final step consolidates rather than celebrates, since the aim is that the hardest situation is now ordinary and the plan can be repeated, and a programme that ended at the top of the ladder without any arrangement for maintenance would leave the person where the ladder started. The order that puts relaxation after the first approach fails because the technique cannot be used where it is needed if it has not been learned. The order that puts the hardest situation before the middle ones fails because the ladder only works upwards.
questions.hint: List before approaching, learn the technique before the first step, and climb only after each step holds.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: Counting the Pupils Below a High Score
questions.learningObjective: convert a standard score into a share below it and then into a head count
questions.stem: A test has a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. Of 200 students, how many would be expected to score below 130?
questions.explanation: A score of 130 is 30 above the mean, and the standard deviation is 15, so it sits two deviations above the mean, and about 97.7 percent of a normal distribution lies below two deviations. Applying that to 200 students gives 0.977 multiplied by 200, which is about 195, leaving roughly five students above that score. The figure is worth computing rather than reading off a table impression, because the answer is close to the whole group and it is easy to expect a much smaller number from a score that sounds impressive. It is also the clearest demonstration of why a high score means rank rather than quantity: being above two deviations from the mean puts a student near the top of almost any class.
questions.hint: Divide the gap from the mean by the standard deviation, read the share below that many deviations, then multiply by 200.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: Ranking Consistently Across Two Occasions
questions.learningObjective: compute the share of participants whose rank band was unchanged
questions.stem: One hundred students take a test twice, two weeks apart, and 60 of them fall in the same half of the score distribution on both occasions. What percentage showed that?
questions.explanation: The share is the 60 who stayed in the same half over the 100 who took the test, so 60 over 100 is 0.6, or 60 percent. Note what the figure does and does not show, because that is the useful part. It shows that most students' standing was stable across two sittings, which is a necessary condition for a score to mean anything. It does not show that the scores themselves were stable, since students can stay in the same half while moving within it, and it is not a reliability coefficient either, because a band is a coarse classification and loses the ordering that a correlation would use. The number is worth computing because a policy such as a resit pass mark depends on how much of a group is likely to move, and a figure of 60 percent is the sort of thing that should be checked rather than assumed.
questions.hint: Divide the number who stayed in the same half by the total who took the test and multiply by 100.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Intelligence, Emotion and Practice: How Well an Item Separates Two Halves
questions.learningObjective: compute an item's discrimination index from the pass rates of two groups
questions.stem: An item is passed by 60 percent of the higher-scoring half of a group and by 40 percent of the lower-scoring half. What is the item's discrimination index?
questions.explanation: The index is the pass rate of the upper half minus the pass rate of the lower half, so 0.60 minus 0.40 gives 0.20. A value of zero would mean the item is passed equally often by strong and weak scorers, which is what a question about a fact everybody knows looks like, and a negative value means the stronger half got it wrong more often, which usually indicates a miskeyed option or a badly worded stem. Computing the index for every item is what makes a test's quality reportable rather than asserted, and an item with a positive index well below the others in a test is a candidate for rewriting. The figure here is modest rather than strong, which is normal for a single item and is why the report describes a test by the pattern across its items rather than by any one of them.
questions.hint: Subtract the lower half's pass rate from the upper half's pass rate.
